Fast Power Indices

CountingAlgebraPermutations
Game: See how much say each member of a real voting body has, like the states choosing a US president.
How to play: Pick a voting body from the list, or change the votes and the number needed to win, and compare each member's share of votes with its share of power.

PlayerWeightBanzhafShapley-Shubik

Look for the math

The two power indices of Weighted Voting and Power Indices are defined by counting: every coalition for Banzhaf, every order of joining for Shapley-Shubik. With the 51 votes of the US Electoral College there are 2⁵¹ coalitions and 51! orders, numbers far too large to list. Yet the answers come back at once.

Counting with polynomials

Multiply out (1 + x^w₁)(1 + x^w₂)…: each term picks, from each bracket, either 1 (the player stays out) or x^w (the player joins), so the coefficient of x^s is the number of coalitions weighing exactly s. This is a generating function. Leave player i out of the product, and player i swings exactly the coalitions of the others that weigh from q − wᵢ to q − 1: adding those coefficients gives the Banzhaf count. Only powers below q matter, so the work is about players × players × quota, not 2ⁿ.

And with a second variable

For Shapley-Shubik the size of the coalition matters too: a swing by a coalition of k others makes player i pivotal in k!(n − 1 − k)! orders. So the applet multiplies (1 + y·x^w) instead and keeps the coefficients by both size and weight. The test compared both indices with plain counting on over 6,000 small systems, and checked the applet's polynomial step for every player of every data set.

What the numbers show

In the Security Council (9 votes needed, each permanent member able to veto) a permanent member has Shapley-Shubik power 421/2145 ≈ 19.6% and a non-permanent member 4/2145 ≈ 0.19%, a hundred times less. In the Electoral College the big states' power is a little more than their share of the votes.

Choose the European Union and raise the quota from 62 towards 87. When do the small countries lose their power?
